About the Reading List

Every week of INFO1113 has a short, prescribed reading, and it's worth taking seriously. The official reading list — with the books and your Library access links — lives on Canvas:

👉 Reading List (Canvas): https://canvas.sydney.edu.au/courses/73747/external_tools/45015?display=borderless

Canvas lists the books, but not the week-by-week breakdown, so the full weekly list is reproduced below for you to work from here on Ed.

Why reading matters in this course

INFO1113 moves quickly from writing procedures to designing objects, and a lot of that shift happens in your head between lectures. Lectures and tutorials show the ideas in motion; the readings are where they settle. A chapter read before the lecture means you arrive already knowing the vocabulary, so the live session becomes reinforcement rather than first contact — and the tutorial becomes practice rather than catch-up.

Reading also builds the understanding you'll be asked to demonstrate directly: the Assignment 2 viva and the final exam reward people who can explain why code is designed a certain way, not just make it run. That fluency comes from reading widely, not only from coding.

How the list works

Each week's reading is split into two kinds:

Core — the set reading. If you do nothing else, do this. It tracks the week's lecture directly.

Stretch (optional) — depth for when you want more, mostly from Effective Java. Not required, but rewarding once the core idea has clicked.

Nobody is ever forced to buy a book: every week's Core is satisfiable from free or library sources. The free MIT 6.031 notes and the JUnit 5 guide carry the testing/specifications/ADT through-line ("the spine"); Big Java is the optional coherent book to follow if you prefer one; Effective Java is Stretch-only.

Sources

BJ — Horstmann, Big Java: Early Objects, 7th ed (ISBN 9781119499091). Anchor text; available as a Library e-book. The 5th ed is an acceptable substitute — same chapter numbers, only page numbers differ (the pages below are for the 7th ed).

6.031 — MIT Software Construction reading notes (sp22). Free, open web: https://web.mit.edu/6.031/www/sp22/

JUnit — JUnit 5 User Guide. Free, open web: https://junit.org/junit5/docs/current/user-guide/

EJ — Bloch, Effective Java, 3rd ed (ISBN 9780134685991). Library e-book; Stretch reading only.

UML — Fowler, UML Distilled, 3rd ed. Library; used for the UML thread.

HFDP — Freeman & Robson, Head First Design Patterns, 2nd ed. Library; Week 12 enrichment (optional).

Weekly topics at a glance

Week 1 — From Procedures to Objects

Week 2 — Designing a Class

Week 3 — References, Identity & Memory

Week 4 — Specifications, Contracts & Testing

Week 5 — Equality, Hashing & Immutability

Week 6 — Interfaces & Subtyping

Week 7 — Implementation Inheritance & its Discontents

Week 8 — Polymorphism & Dynamic Dispatch

Week 9 — Generics

Week 10 — Collections & ADTs

Week 11 — Exceptions & Error Handling

Week 12 — Assignment 2 Studio (no required reading)

Week 13 — Review, Synthesis & Exam Prep (no new reading)

The full reading for each week is listed below.

Week-by-week detail

Week 1 — From Procedures to Objects

Core: BJ Ch 1 (Introduction), Ch 2 (Using Objects), Ch 3 (Implementing Classes — fields, methods, constructors); Ch 4 (Fundamental Data Types) as a Python→Java typing reference.

Stretch: —

Week 2 — Designing a Class

Core: BJ Ch 3 + Ch 8 (Designing Classes — encapsulation, cohesion); 6.031 Specifications (intro — what a contract is; the spine begins).

Stretch: EJ Item 15 (minimise accessibility), Item 16 (use accessor methods).

Week 3 — References, Identity & Memory

Core: BJ Ch 8 §Object References + Ch 2; 6.031 Mutability & Immutability (§aliasing).

Stretch: EJ Item 50 (make defensive copies).

Week 4 — Specifications, Contracts & Testing

Core: 6.031 Testing + Specifications + Designing Specifications; JUnit Writing Tests + Assertions; BJ Ch 8 §Unit Testing + §Preconditions and Postconditions.

Stretch: 6.031 Debugging — the "read the failure" ladder.

Week 5 — Equality, Hashing & Immutability

Core: BJ Ch 9 §overriding equals + Ch 15 §hashCode/HashMap; 6.031 Equality + Mutability & Immutability.

Stretch: EJ Items 10 (obey the equals contract), 11 (always override hashCode), 17 (minimise mutability), 50 (defensive copies).

Week 6 — Interfaces & Subtyping

Core: BJ Ch 10 (Interfaces) — read before Ch 9 + Ch 14 §Comparator; 6.031 Interfaces, Generics & Enums (§interfaces); UML class diagrams + BJ Ch 12 §UML.

Stretch: EJ Items 20 (prefer interfaces to abstract classes), 64 (refer to objects by their interfaces), 14 (consider implementing Comparable).

Week 7 — Implementation Inheritance & its Discontents

Core: BJ Ch 9 (Inheritance — extends, super, override, abstract classes, constructor chaining).

Stretch: EJ Items 18 (favour composition over inheritance), 19 (design and document for inheritance or else prohibit it) — the fragile-base-class canon.

Week 8 — Polymorphism & Dynamic Dispatch

Core: BJ Ch 9 §Polymorphism / Dynamic Method Lookup + Ch 10; 6.031 Recursion or BJ Ch 13 (recursion touchpoint).

Stretch: EJ Item 52 (use overloading judiciously — override vs overload).

Week 9 — Generics

Core: BJ Ch 18 (Generic Classes) + Ch 7 §diamond syntax; 6.031 Interfaces, Generics & Enums (§generics).

Stretch: EJ Items 26 (don't use raw types), 29 (favour generic types), 30 (favour generic methods), 31 (use bounded wildcards to increase API flexibility).

Week 10 — Collections & ADTs

Core: BJ Ch 15 (Collections Framework) + Ch 16 (Basic Data Structures) + Ch 17 (Tree Structures — recursion touchpoint); 6.031 Abstract Data Types + Abstraction Functions & Rep Invariants; light: BJ Ch 19 (Stream Processing) for map/filter/reduce.

Stretch: EJ Item 47 (prefer Collection to Stream as a return type); Big-O reasoning about structure choice.

Week 11 — Exceptions & Error Handling

Core: BJ Ch 11 (Input/Output and Exception Handling — try/catch/finally, checked vs unchecked); JUnit assertThrows (negative testing).

Stretch: EJ Items 69 (use exceptions only for exceptional conditions), 70 (checked for recoverable, runtime for programming errors), 72 (favour standard exceptions), 73 (throw exceptions appropriate to the abstraction).

Week 12 — Assignment 2 Studio (light)

This week: no required reading — it's an Assignment 2 studio week.

Optional self-study (not examined): HFDP Head First Design Patterns — Strategy, Observer, Decorator, Factory, Iterator/Composite chapters. Gamma et al., Design Patterns (GoF) — reference only.

Week 13 — Review, Synthesis & Exam Prep

Core: No new reading. Re-walk the spine: 6.031 Testing / Specifications / Abstract Data Types.

Stretch: EJ skim the Items flagged across Weeks 5–11.

Cross-cutting threads (not single weeks)

Recursion (W3, W8, W10): 6.031 Recursion; BJ Ch 13.

Debugging / reading failures (every week): 6.031 Debugging.

UML & design documents (W2, W6, exam): UML Fowler; BJ Ch 12.

You don't need to read everything cover to cover. Follow the weekly Core list, dip into Stretch when a topic grabs you, and prepare before each lecture. It's one of the highest-return habits you can build this semester.

About Drills

Drills are short, in-class activities you complete during your tutorial most weeks. They're worth 10% of your final course mark, and they're designed to keep you practising the current material as it's introduced — little and often, rather than cramming. Drills are formative and are not a hurdle: they contribute to your mark, but they can't stop you passing the unit. The goal is your learning and genuine effort, not getting every answer right.

How a normal drill week works

Your tutor hands out (or displays) the week's drill, and you complete it in class.

Once time is up, your tutor goes through the answers with the room.

Your tutor photographs the completed drills of the students who are present.

You then upload your photo to SRES so it's recorded against your name: 
Please use the link and QR code on the sheet itself. Each week is different

That's it — attend, have a genuine go, and upload your photo.

Your tutor will be taking attendance and a photo of your attempt. These will be used toward the grade.

Weeks 7 and 12: your own personalised quiz (built with AI)

Twice in the semester — in Week 7 and Week 12 — the drill is a little different. Instead of a quiz we give you, you create your own.

The idea is to target the things you find hard, and — importantly — to build it with AI. We want you to lean into AI tools as much as possible here: use any AI tool you like to generate a short, personalised quiz on the concepts you feel least confident about. Learning to direct an AI tool well is a genuine skill, and this is your chance to practise it.

The recommended workflow: photograph all your earlier drills, hand them (and the concepts you keep getting wrong) to an AI tool, and ask it to build you a new quiz of exactly those tricky questions. A template you can hand straight to an AI is provided — fill in your details and your weak topics, paste it into the tool with your materials, and let it do the rest: 

You must include a reference. Whatever AI tool you use, record it on your quiz (the template has a Reference field) — the tool's name and version, and one line on how you used it. Acknowledging your AI use honestly is part of the task and of the University's academic integrity expectations.

Prefer not to use AI? That's allowed. You can build your quiz from your own knowledge, or with help from tutors, classmates, or online resources instead — but you still must produce a genuine personalisation, and you still must fill in the Reference field with exactly what you used. The one thing you can't do is hand in a generic quiz that isn't personalised to you.

On the day:

Bring a blank, printed copy of your personalised quiz to the tutorial.

Complete it in class, in front of your tutor, during the drill.

Hand it in to your tutor at the end.

How your drills mark is worked out (out of 10)

Three simple pieces that add up:

Ordinary weekly drills — 1 mark each, up to 6. A drill counts when you attend, attempt at least three questions, and upload it by the Friday deadline. Six counted drills gives you the full 6 — doing more doesn't add marks.

Week 7 personalised quiz — up to 2 marks.

Week 12 personalised quiz — up to 2 marks.

Each personalised quiz mark is your tutor's view of a genuine, personalised effort with your Reference filled in (0 if it isn't done or isn't a real personalisation). Missed your week? Do it in the makeup week — Week 8 for Week 7, Week 13 for Week 12. Miss a quiz and its makeup and that quiz scores 0.

Across the whole semester we also ask for at least 6 correct answers in total — a low bar that just shows you're genuinely having a go.

Your total is out of 10. For example:

6 ordinary drills + both quizzes done well → 6 + 2 + 2 = 10/10.

4 ordinary drills + both quizzes → 4 + 4 = 8/10.

6 ordinary drills, no personalised quizzes → 6/10.

Common questions

Does the drill count if I'm absent from the tutorial?

No — drills are completed and marked in class, so you need to be there that week for it to count.

What if I miss a week?

You just don't earn that week's mark — and since you only need 6 counted drills for the full weekly portion, a couple of misses may not cost you anything. Because drills aren't a hurdle, missing more won't stop you passing either.

What if I'm absent in Week 7 or Week 12 (the personalised quiz)?

You can complete it in the following week instead — Week 8 or Week 13. If you miss both weeks of a pair (7 and 8, or 12 and 13), you simply don't earn that quiz's marks (up to 2). It won't stop you passing.

Is there Special Consideration or Simple Extension for drills?

Unfortunately not — drills are a weekly, contemporaneous assessment completed live in class, so they aren't eligible for a Simple Extension or Special Consideration. The good news is that they're only 10%, they're not a hurdle, and the mark scale is forgiving: you don't need a perfect run of weeks to do well.

What if I don't answer very well?

That's completely fine. Drills are formative — your mark comes from your participation and your Week 7 and Week 12 quizzes, not from getting everything correct. Any genuine effort you make contributes to your mark, so don't stress about perfect answers.

If anything here is unclear, please ask on Ed before the next tutorial.

John

Hi everyone,

I'm John, and I'm really looking forward to teaching you this semester. Whether this is your first time writing code or you've been at it for a while, you're in the right place.

Ed Discussion is our home base for the course, but it works a little differently here, so it's worth reading how before you dive in.

How our Ed works

There are two kinds of posts: staff posts and student posts.

Staff posts — announcements and FAQ posts — are our official channel. This is where the real course information lives, so read every staff announcement and check the FAQ posts regularly. FAQs are organised by week in reverse order (current week first), with questions numbered sequentially, so recent topics are always right at the top.

Student posts are your space to ask and help each other. We don't reply to individual student posts one by one — instead, staff monitor everything and publish FAQ responses every few days that answer the common questions in one place, so everyone benefits. Your classmates are strongly encouraged to jump in and help, and honestly, that's where a lot of the best learning happens.

A quick, honest note: the teaching team is small relative to the size of the class. Bundling answers into FAQs is how we make sure everyone gets the information rather than only the fastest few — so if you don't get a direct reply, that's by design, not because you've been missed.

Heart posts you find useful so the best ones rise to the top.

Answer classmates when you know something. Explaining it is one of the best ways to lock it in for yourself.

Personal or administrative questions (not course content) → email info1113.2026-s2@sydney.edu.au and allow up to four working days for a reply.

Ask early, ask often, help each other out — and let's make this a great semester.

(a) State what must always be true about that running state -- the

facts about the current time and the current venue that the rest

of your code relies on never being broken.





For the current time, it always represents the end time of the most recently scheduled activity.  

Therefore, the current time must always be greater than or equal to the startTime of the previous scheduled activity and less than MINUTES_PER_DAY. 



For the current venue, it always represents the location of the most recently scheduled activity. 

The venue must always be one of the three valid locations: HOME, UNI, or CITY.(I did not include this verification in the program)



(b) Name one place in your own code, by class and method, where one

of those facts could be broken, and say what stops that from

happening.



One place where the time invariant could be broken is in DayQuest.main(), during the schedule-building loop. 

The Activity class allows an activity object to exist even if its end time is after midnight. 

Therefore, this is prevented by schedule builderin DayQuest.main(). 

Before updating the current time(schedule the activity), the program checks whether the activity ends before midnight. 

If the activity would end after midnight, the program uses return to stop the scheduling process. 

As a result, currentTime is never updated to an invalid value, and the invariant is preserved throughout schedule construction.

For the current time to be be greater than or equal to the startTime of the previously scheduled, this part is protected by the Activity class constructor,
